results.name: Gold ring
results.description:
**Collection:** Prehistory and Historical Archeology Dept.

**Inv.-No.:** [UF-19884.377](https://www.online.landessammlungen-noe.at/objects/1009549)

**Material:** Gold

**Dimensions:** 1,43 x 2,36 cm

**Dating:** 150-350 CE

The piece of jewellery under consideration is a large gold ring in the shape of two intertwined snakes.
The ring was crafted in a distinctive meandering shape and featured snake heads at the ends as decorative embellishments. The presence of small knots is observable at the points where the meanders intersect. The scales of the plastic snake heads have been meticulously crafted to display a realism in their appearance. In the area where the ocular cavities should be located, it is presumed that gemstones or glass were inserted.

This object was digitized through the ‘Kulturerbe digital’ program of the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, Public Service and Sport.

results.name: Biscuit And Clasp EOA:2022.185.2
results.description:
'Biscuit' and clasp concretion from the wreck of the Earl Of Abergavenny.

ID: EOA:2022.185.2  OE445

Collection: Earl of Abergavenny

Classification: Crew/passenger

Measurements: Coin Diametre 45mm Clasp Length 25mm Width 15mm

Date made: as yet unknown

Display: not on display

Manufacturer/Creator: as yet unknown

Credit: Portland Museum Trust

Generally known as a biscuit, due to the process of oxidisation that has led to its current form and appearance, this eight reale coin, also known as a piece of eight, has become attached to a garnet encrusted clasp, possibly from a piece of jewellery belonging to one of the ship's passengers.

For more information about the Diving into the Digital Archives of the Earl of Abergavenny project click [here](http://portlandmuseum.co.uk/earl-of-abergavenny/)

results.name: Roman Stone Mortar
results.description:
Everyday life in Pontes, Roman Staines - a stone mortar fabricated from Purbeck burr stone (broken shell limestone). Similar mortars are found at Silchester and Londinium. This may well have been used for food preparation, but may also have been used for grinding pigments for wall painting or enamel for jewellery.

This item was found at the Barclays bank site in 1969. It was recovered by workmen as part of their normal operations, so the context of this find is unclear. The item was reconstructed, probably by the lead archaeologist Maureen Rendell. 

The mortar dimensions (mm) are: Extreme diameter at rim over lugs 178, Outer diameter at rim apart from  lugs 150, Inner diameter at rim 118, Outer diameter of base 150, Inner diameter of base 95, Outer height rim to base 45-48, Maximum depth rim to inner base 38, Inner depth rim to wall junction 32, Breadth of lug 25 and 30, Height of lug 16 and 12.

This mortar is currently on display at Spelthorne Museum.

results.name: Torc with imitation buffers
results.description:
**Collection:** Prehistory and Historical Archeology Dept.

**Inv.-No.:** [UF-23056.107](https://www.online.landessammlungen-noe.at/objects/1436448)

**Material:** Bronze

**Dimensions:** 13,69 cm

**Dating:** 375-260 BCE

The bronze torc is composed of two components. The front of the object features a cylindrical, box-shaped decorative piece situated centrally, with two conical buffer ends that join together. This piece has eyelets on both sides into which the bronze pins on the two wire ends can be fixed with a plug-in fastener. The front of the ring features an ornamental decoration. The sides of the imitation buffer ends illustrate radiant projections. The following spherical sections also exhibit ornamentation, which become faded over time. A noteworthy finding is that the wire displays distinctive S-shaped spirals exclusively within the front section.

This object was digitized through the ‘Kulturerbe digital’ program of the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, Public Service and Sport.

results.name: Silver Ring (NHMW-PRAE-SH419c-01)
results.description:
3D model of a silver ring that forms part of a precious jewelry set in Suebian/Germanic style from a woman’s grave presumably found at Mount Oberleis in Lower Austria, just north of the boundary of the former Roman Empire. Germanic tribes settled there at the time when close to the military fort of Carnuntum the [“Heidentor” (aka “Heathens' Gate”, Austria’s contribution to Europeana Twin it!)](https://kulturpool.at/inhalte/die-europaeische-kampagne-twin-it-zur-3d-digitalisierung) was erected during the reign of the roman emperor, Constantinus II. These tribes were often allied with the Romans south of the Danube and strongly influenced by their culture.

On display in Hall 13 of the NHM Vienna.

**Object**: Silver ring

**Inventory number:** NHMW-PRAE-SH419c-01

**Collection:** NHM Vienna, Department of Prehistory (curator: Stefan Eichert)

[More about the NHM Vienna](www.nhm.at)

Digitized using microCT imaging (YXLON FF35 CT) and edited in ORS Dragonfly and Blender by Viola Winkler (NHMW)
